output.myth: Ennu the Kite-Wright kept a bone awl for her sailcloth, and was proud of it, the way you are proud of a tool that never splits a seam. One cold season Aun came down the cliff with a torn sail and no patience, and asked to borrow it. She lent it. He pushed it through the cloth so hard the point went out the far side and kept going, through the weave, through the wind, until it stuck in the Upper Sea. The handle caught on the rim of Vel and never came free. Hesk, who keeps count, says the holes it made are the ring of small stars. When a boat-mender lays her pattern on the cloth before lacing, she is only copying the marks the awl left above. Mend what you can. Return what you borrow. The point still has the sail on it, and Aun has been meaning to fetch it for a long time.
output.verse:
Hold the awl, mend the
torn sail, count the holes in Vel:
